title: Portable consumers over filesystem and subprocess execution worlds
summary: The filesystem service and the subprocess service together define one execution world; terminals, language servers and shells consume those two interfaces instead of host APIs, so a remote provider needs no separate terminal or language-server package.
firstReason: This is what lets SSH and sandboxed execution work without duplicating consumers; the Go design should define the same two interfaces.

title: Subprocess control pipe
summary: A subprocess can be given a dedicated control pipe on file descriptor 7, separate from standard output and error, so a host protocol never mixes with program output; consumers own the framing.
firstReason: A separate control channel is needed for the same reason in Go and is supported by passing extra files to the child process; the Windows handle-inheritance details need their own Go implementation.

title: A seen prompt marker keeps its own tail grace
summary: The persistent terminal gains a `promptTailGraceMs` setting (default 0). After the prompt marker has been seen but its printable tail has not arrived, the readiness wait is extended by that amount, because the Windows pseudo-terminal delivers the marker and the prompt text in two chunks.
firstReason: The two-chunk delivery comes from the Windows console layer, not from Node, so a Go pseudo-terminal sees it too. A default of zero keeps the behaviour opt-in; the terminal area should measure the right value again with its Go PTY library.

title: Windows persistent PTYs use the console host node-pty ships
summary: On Windows, persistent terminals are allocated with the OpenConsole binary that the node-pty package ships (`useConptyDll: true`) instead of the console host of the operating system, because the system console host on one test machine did not render the prompt reliably.
firstReason: The finding (the operating system's console host can be too old to render prompts reliably) stands, but the fix is a node-pty option. The Go design must choose a PTY library and decide whether to ship its own console host with it.

title: persistent PTY sessions
summary: An optional capability family gives an agent persistent, line-oriented pseudo-terminal sessions that survive across tool calls, exposed through six `terminal_*` tools. A service defines the session contract and a backend runs a persistent shell with readiness detection and bounded buffers; full-screen applications and restoring a session after its process is lost are deferred.
firstReason: Workflows whose state lives in a terminal (debuggers, REPLs, activated environments) need it, and it follows the capability-seam pattern the Go design keeps. The Go design needs its own PTY library choice.

title: Remove the E2B execution providers
summary: The three providers that ran files, commands and terminals in an E2B cloud sandbox were removed. Remote execution stays an intended capability: the filesystem and subprocess contracts remain asynchronous and provider-neutral so that a remote backend can be added without changing tools.
firstReason: The Go design should likewise ship no E2B backend and keep the contracts remote-capable, which the SSH providers already require. The removal still holds in Go: the blocker was a missing control channel in the vendor SDK, not anything in JavaScript.

title: Keep shell-environment declarations focused on key ownership
summary: Proposal: a plugin that contributes shell environment variables declares only the names it owns; the per-variable descriptions and the method that lists them are removed because nothing reads them.
firstReason: Adopt: key ownership, conflict detection and refusal of undeclared output are the parts with consumers. The Go registry can start with a set of keys per contributor.
